13570:
To relocate means to move from one place to another — and to then set up your life, work, or presence at that new place as your new base.

The key idea is not just movement, but re-establishing yourself somewhere new. When you relocate, the new place becomes your new home, your new headquarters, or your new base of operations.
Two Ways to Use It

Relocate works in two ways depending on who is doing the moving.

1. When the subject moves itself (no object needed)

Here, the person, animal, or organization does the relocating on their own.

She relocated to Germany for her new job.
The company relocated from Mumbai to Pune.
He is planning to relocate next year.

2. When someone moves something or someone else (with an object)

Here, one party moves another — the subject causes the relocation.

The government relocated the flood-affected families to a safer area.
The organization relocated its headquarters to a bigger city.
Wildlife officers relocated the tiger to a national park.
What Makes "Relocate" Different from Just "Move"

This is an important distinction.

"Move" is a broad, everyday word. You can "move" a pen from one side of your desk to the other. You can "move" a chair. It covers any kind of physical movement, big or small, temporary or permanent.

"Relocate" is more specific and more formal. It carries these built-in ideas:

  • The move is significant — usually to a different city, country, or at least a meaningfully different place. You would not say you "relocated" your pen.
  • The new place becomes a new base — somewhere you will live, work, or operate from for a substantial period. It is not a weekend trip or a vacation.
  • The word feels deliberate and purposeful — there is a reason behind the move, usually related to work, safety, opportunity, or necessity.
  • It is more formal in tone than "move" — you will see it more often in news articles, business communication, official documents, and professional conversations.

Think of it this way: every relocation involves movement, but not every movement is a relocation.
Who or What Can Relocate?

People — individuals, families, employees, communities

Thousands of people relocated after the factory shut down.

Organizations — companies, offices, schools, government departments

The startup relocated its office to a co-working space downtown.

Animals — especially in wildlife and conservation contexts

Rangers relocated the herd to a protected forest.

Things — especially places of business or institutions

The clinic has relocated to the new hospital building.
Voluntary vs. Forced Relocation

Relocation can be either a choice or something imposed on someone.

Voluntary relocation — a person or organization chooses to move for a better opportunity, lower costs, personal reasons, etc.

She voluntarily relocated to London to advance her career.

Forced relocation — people are made to move, often due to disasters, conflict, government decisions, or development projects.

The villagers were forcibly relocated to make way for the dam.

Both uses are correct and common.
The Sense of Permanence

Relocating usually implies a long-term or permanent change of base, not a short-term stay. If someone goes somewhere for two weeks, we would not say they "relocated." But if they move there to live and work for the foreseeable future, "relocate" fits perfectly.

That said, in a business context, "relocating an office" might be more about a change of address than about permanence — the emphasis shifts to the establishment of a new operational base, even if the organization might move again someday.
Common Phrases and Collocations

These are word combinations you will frequently see with "relocate":

  • relocate to (a place) — She relocated to New Zealand.
  • relocate from (a place) — They relocated from a small town.
  • relocate for (a reason) — He relocated for work / for family / for health.
  • considering relocating — Are you considering relocating?
  • forced to relocate — They were forced to relocate due to rising rents.
  • help someone relocate — The company helped the new employee relocate.
  • recently relocated — The store has recently relocated.
Related Word Forms

• Relocation (noun) — the act or process of relocating

    The relocation was smooth and well-organized.
    She received a relocation package from her employer.

  • Relocated (past tense / adjective) — describes someone or something that has already moved

    The relocated families are adjusting to their new homes.

  • Relocating (present participle) — describes the ongoing process

    Relocating abroad is a major life decision.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

Understanding similar words will sharpen your understanding of "relocate."

Move — broader, more casual, used for anything from shifting furniture to changing countries. "Relocate" is a more formal, specific subset of "move."

Transfer — usually means moving within the same organization or system, often decided by an employer. A person is "transferred" to another branch by their company. They "relocate" describes the physical act of moving to the new city as a result.

He was transferred to the Delhi office, so the whole family had to relocate.

Migrate — typically refers to large-scale movement of groups (people or animals), often driven by seasonal patterns, economic pressure, or hardship. It has a broader, more sociological feel.

Resettle — often used specifically for refugees, displaced communities, or people who have been uprooted from their homes and are being given a new permanent home. It has a humanitarian connotation.

Uproot — usually figurative and emotional. It implies being torn away from a familiar place, often painfully.
The Register (Formality Level)

Relocate sits in the formal to semi-formal register. You will hear and read it in:

  • Professional and corporate settings ("The team will relocate to the new campus next quarter.")
  • News and journalism ("Over a million people were relocated after the floods.")
  • Official and government language
  • Real estate and HR contexts ("relocation assistance," "relocation package")

In casual everyday speech, most people simply say "move" — "We're moving to Chennai next month." But "relocate" would not sound out of place even in conversation when you want to sound precise or professional.
A Few Final Sentences to Cement It

After losing his job, he decided to relocate to a city with more opportunities.
The headquarters was relocated from a rented office to a building the company now owns.
Relocating is exciting, but it also means leaving behind everything familiar.
The government offered financial support to help displaced residents relocate.
She had always wanted to relocate to the mountains and finally made it happen.

In short: to relocate means to move — deliberately, significantly, and with the intention of making the new place your base — whether that applies to a person, an organization, or any entity that has a "place" it operates from.
13571:
Reluctance is the feeling of not wanting to do something — an inner pull-back, a kind of resistance inside you. It is the uncomfortable sense that you would rather not do something, even though you might still end up doing it.

That last part is crucial, so let's hold it for a moment.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

Reluctance does not mean you refuse to do something. It does not mean you cannot do something. It means you don't want to — but you may do it anyway.

This is what makes "reluctance" so interesting and precise. It captures a specific human experience: the gap between what you feel inside and what you actually do. There is an internal conflict at the heart of this word.

For example:

  • A child feels reluctance about going to bed but eventually goes.
  • A doctor feels reluctance before delivering bad news to a patient but tells them anyway.
  • You might feel reluctance about lending money to a friend — you don't want to, but you do it.

In every case, the person acts, but they act against their own desire or comfort. Reluctance is that feeling of dragging yourself toward something.

When someone experiences reluctance, they typically feel one or more of the following:

  • Unwillingness — a genuine desire to avoid the thing
  • Hesitation — a slowing down before doing it, like a pause before a cold shower
  • Discomfort — a mild sense of dread or resistance
  • Inner conflict — part of them knows they should do it (or must do it), while another part resists

Reluctance is an emotional and mental state. You cannot see it directly — but you can sense it in someone's body language, their slowness, their sighs, or the way they say "Fine, I'll do it."

Reluctance can be mild or strong. The word itself doesn't fix an intensity — context and modifiers do.

  • Mild reluctance: "She agreed to help, but with some reluctance." (She wasn't thrilled, but it wasn't a big deal.)
  • Strong reluctance: "He spoke with great reluctance about his past." (It was clearly painful and very hard for him to do.)
  • Visible reluctance: "She helped, but her reluctance was obvious from her expression." (You could see on her face that she didn't want to.)

You'll often see reluctance paired with words like some, slight, mild, deep, great, obvious, clear, visible, understandable, or considerable.

Here are examples that show how "reluctance" works naturally in real use:

  1. "He accepted the offer, but not without reluctance." (He said yes, but it wasn't easy for him.)
  2. "There is a reluctance among many people to talk about money." (People generally don't want to discuss it.)
  3. "She finally spoke up, overcoming her reluctance." (She pushed past her inner resistance and did it.)
  4. "The government showed reluctance to change the law." (It was unwilling to act, though it could.)
  5. "With visible reluctance, he handed over his phone." (You could see he didn't want to, but he did.)
  6. "Her reluctance to get involved was understandable." (It made sense that she didn't want to step in.)

Notice how in every sentence, reluctance describes an inner state — not the act itself. The act may or may not follow, but the feeling is always there.

Certain phrases with "reluctance" come up again and again in English:

  • "with reluctance" — doing something, but unwillingly: "She left with reluctance."
  • "with great reluctance" — doing something very unwillingly: "He admitted it with great reluctance."
  • "show reluctance" — to display unwillingness: "The team showed reluctance to adopt the new system."
  • "overcome reluctance" — to push past that inner resistance: "She overcame her reluctance and asked for help."
  • "express reluctance" — to communicate that you don't want to do something: "He expressed reluctance about signing the contract."
  • "without reluctance" — doing something easily and willingly: "She agreed without reluctance." (This often signals that something was surprisingly easy or comfortable for someone.)

It helps to understand what reluctance does not mean, to sharpen the picture:

Reluctance ≠ Refusal.
Refusal means you won't do it, full stop. Reluctance means you don't want to, but you might still do it. A person refuses a request. A person feels reluctance about a task they're about to do.

Reluctance ≠ Inability.
"I can't do it" is inability. "I don't want to do it, but I will" is reluctance. Reluctance is always about willingness, never about capacity.

Reluctance ≠ Laziness.
Laziness is about not making an effort due to lack of motivation or energy. Reluctance is specifically about not wanting to do a particular thing — often because it feels uncomfortable, risky, painful, or unpleasant. A hardworking person can feel reluctance. A lazy person may simply not care enough to try at all.

Reluctance ≠ Fear.
Fear is a specific emotion. Reluctance is broader. You can feel reluctance without being afraid — for example, being reluctant to apologise (not because you fear it, but because it bruises your ego). That said, fear can be one of the causes of reluctance.

Reluctance comes from many sources. Understanding these helps you use the word more precisely:

  • Discomfort — something feels unpleasant or awkward (reluctance to visit the dentist)
  • Risk or uncertainty — something feels unsafe or unknown (reluctance to invest money)
  • Loss — doing the thing means giving something up (reluctance to leave a job you love)
  • Principle or conscience — something doesn't feel right to you (reluctance to lie, even to protect someone)
  • Pride or ego — something feels humbling (reluctance to admit you were wrong)
  • Habit or inertia — it's hard to change, so you resist (reluctance to adopt a new routine)

In physics, the word "reluctance" has a completely separate, technical meaning — it refers to resistance to magnetic flux in a circuit. This meaning has nothing to do with feelings or emotions. If you encounter "reluctance" in a physics textbook, it is an entirely different concept. But in everyday life and in literature, the word always means the emotional/mental state described above.

Reluctance is the feeling of not wanting to do something. It is an inner resistance — not a refusal, not an inability, but an unwillingness. A reluctant person may still act, but they do so against the grain of their own comfort or desire.

If you can hold that idea — inner resistance that doesn't necessarily stop action — you have grasped the word completely.
13572:
Reluctant means you don't want to do something, but you are not completely refusing either. There is a quiet resistance inside you — a feeling that pulls you away from doing something, even if you end up doing it anyway.

Think of it this way: imagine someone asks you to speak in front of a large crowd. You are nervous, you'd rather not do it, but your boss is counting on you, so you agree. In that moment, you are reluctant. You are not saying "absolutely no." You are saying "I really don't want to, but... fine."

This inner tug-of-war is the heart of the word.

The most important thing to understand about reluctant is what it is not:

  • It does not mean you flatly refuse.
  • It does not mean you are simply slow or lazy.
  • It does not mean you are confused about what to do.

It specifically means you have a real, felt discomfort or unwillingness toward something, but you have not fully blocked it out. You may still do the thing. You just don't want to.

This is why reluctant is such a rich and honest word — it captures that very human feeling of doing something against your own wishes.

These examples will show you how the word actually lives in the real world:

  • She was reluctant to forgive him, but eventually she did.

Here, she didn't want to forgive him. The feeling was real. But she came around. The word tells you about her inner resistance, not what she finally chose.

  • He gave a reluctant nod.

He nodded, yes — but clearly not happily. You can feel the effort it took.

  • The child was reluctant to go to bed.

Classic. The child wants to stay up, doesn't want to sleep, and resists — even if they eventually shuffle off to their room.

  • She was a reluctant hero.

This is a very common phrase. It means she never wanted to be a hero. The role was pushed onto her. She stepped up, but not because she craved it.

  • He reluctantly agreed to help.

(Here it is used as the adverb reluctantly, but notice the meaning: he agreed, but with visible unwillingness.)

Reluctance is not always the same strength. It can be mild or intense:

Mild reluctance — a small hesitation, a slight preference against something. Like being reluctant to wake up early on a weekend.

Strong reluctance — a deep, serious unwillingness, where doing the thing feels genuinely hard. Like a whistleblower who is reluctant to speak up because they fear the consequences, but they know it's the right thing.

In both cases, the word fits. Context tells you how strong the feeling is.
How It Is Used With Other Words

Reluctant almost always appears in one of these two patterns:

Pattern 1: reluctant + to + verb
This tells you what the person doesn't want to do.

  • reluctant to admit a mistake
  • reluctant to leave a comfortable job
  • reluctant to speak about the past
  • reluctant to accept help

Pattern 2: reluctant + noun
Here, the word describes the person or thing itself as unwilling.

  • a reluctant participant
  • a reluctant ally
  • a reluctant smile (a smile that came only after resistance — touching and real)
  • a reluctant decision
Closely Related Words (And How They Differ)

Understanding nearby words will sharpen your understanding of reluctant even further.

Unwilling — Stronger than reluctant. "Unwilling" often sounds more final, like a door that is shut. "Reluctant" sounds more like a door that is half-open. He was unwilling to talk = hard no. He was reluctant to talk = he didn't want to, but he might.

Hesitant — This is more about uncertainty or lack of confidence. A hesitant person might not know what to do, or might be nervous. A reluctant person knows what they're being asked — they just don't want to do it.

Resistant — This is more active and can imply pushing back or fighting against something. Reluctance is quieter, more internal. Resistance can be outward.

Grudging — Very close to reluctant, but grudging carries a stronger sense of bitterness or resentment. A grudging compliment is given painfully. A reluctant compliment is given after some hesitation, but without necessarily the sting of resentment.
The opposite of reluctant is willing, eager, or enthusiastic — someone who wants to do something, who leans toward it rather than away from it.

Since you're learning the adjective, it helps to know the full family:

  • Reluctance (noun) — the feeling of not wanting to do something. "She agreed with great reluctance."
  • Reluctantly (adverb) — describes how something is done, when it is done against one's wishes. "He reluctantly handed over the keys."
The Single Best Way to Remember It

Picture someone dragging their feet. They are moving forward, yes — but every step is heavy, slow, and against their own desire. That image is reluctance. The feet move, but the heart pulls back.

Whenever you use reluctant, ask yourself: Is this person being pulled in two directions — away from something, yet still possibly doing it? If yes, the word fits perfectly.
13573:
"Reluctantly" means doing something without wanting to, but doing it anyway.

There are two things happening at the same time when someone does something reluctantly:

  1. Inside, they don't want to do it — they resist, hesitate, or wish they didn't have to.
  2. Outside, they still go ahead and do it — perhaps because they feel they must.

That gap between not wanting to and still doing it — that is the heart of "reluctantly."

Imagine a child who hates vegetables. His mother tells him he can't leave the dinner table until he finishes his broccoli. He stares at it, makes a face, pushes it around the plate — but eventually, slowly, he picks up his fork and eats it.

He ate the broccoli reluctantly.

He didn't want to. He resisted. But in the end, he did it.
What Kind of Word It Is (and How It Works)

"Reluctantly" is an adverb. That means it describes how an action is done. It answers the question: "In what way did they do it?"

It almost always sits right next to the action (the verb) it is describing:

  • She reluctantly signed the contract.
  • He reluctantly agreed to help.
  • They reluctantly canceled the trip.
  • Reluctantly, she handed over her phone.

In each case, the action happened — but it happened with inner resistance.
Why Do People Do Things Reluctantly?

There are many reasons someone might act reluctantly. The feeling of not wanting to do something can come from:

  • Obligation or duty: A doctor reluctantly tells a patient bad news. It's his job, and he must — but he wishes he didn't have to.
  • Social pressure: You reluctantly agree to attend a boring party because a close friend really wants you there.
  • Logic overruling preference: She reluctantly sold her old car when she ran out of money. She loved that car, but she had no choice.
  • Admitting something uncomfortable: He reluctantly admitted that he was wrong. It hurt his pride, but the evidence was clear.
  • Going along with a decision you disagree with: The team reluctantly accepted the new policy, even though they all felt it was unfair.

In every case, something pushes the person to act — duty, need, reason, or circumstance — even though their inner feeling is pulling the other way.
The Level of Reluctance Can Vary

"Reluctantly" does not always mean extreme unwillingness. It can describe a whole range, from mild to strong:

  • Mild: "I reluctantly skipped my morning run because it was raining." — Just a small disappointment; not a big deal.
  • Moderate: "She reluctantly agreed to work late on a Friday." — She really didn't want to, but she said yes.
  • Strong: "The government reluctantly passed the controversial law after years of pressure." — There was deep, serious resistance before this happened.

The word itself doesn't tell you exactly how reluctant someone was — context does that.

This is important for getting the word exactly right:

It does NOT mean the person refused. The action still happened. If someone refused, you would not use "reluctantly" to describe that refusal. "Reluctantly" always describes a completed action — one that happened despite the unwillingness.

  • ✅ "He reluctantly ate the food." — He didn't want to, but he ate it.
  • ❌ "He reluctantly refused the food." — This doesn't work. "Reluctantly refused" would mean he didn't even want to refuse — which would need a very specific context to make sense.

It does NOT mean forced against one's will. When someone does something reluctantly, they still make a choice — it's just not the choice they would prefer. If a person is physically forced into something with no choice at all, "reluctantly" is too weak a word.
Similar Words — and How They Differ

Understanding nearby words helps sharpen your understanding:

Willingly — the direct opposite. Doing something with desire, openness, or enthusiasm. "She willingly stayed late to help her colleague." No resistance at all.

Grudgingly — a stronger, harsher version of reluctantly. When you do something grudgingly, you do it with bitterness or resentment — almost like you're silently protesting while doing it. A worker who feels he's being treated unfairly might grudgingly follow his manager's orders, feeling angry the whole time. "Reluctantly" is gentler; "grudgingly" has more of an edge of bitterness.

Hesitantly — related, but different. "Hesitantly" is about uncertainty or nervousness — pausing, being unsure. Someone can hesitate because they're nervous, confused, or careful — not necessarily because they don't want to. You might hesitantly knock on the door of someone important because you're nervous, while you might reluctantly knock because you don't want to have that conversation at all.

Here are examples that show how widely this word is used:

  • In everyday life: "I reluctantly woke up at 5 a.m. for my early flight." — Wished I could sleep, but I had to.
  • In relationships: "He reluctantly forgave his friend after the argument." — It wasn't easy, but he did it.
  • In business: "The company reluctantly lowered its prices after losing customers." — They didn't want to, but had to.
  • In politics: "The leader reluctantly stepped down after mounting criticism." — He held on as long as he could, but eventually gave way.
  • In personal growth: "She reluctantly accepted that she needed help and finally called a therapist." — Pride made it hard, but she did the right thing.
  • In small decisions: "He reluctantly let his younger sister choose the movie." — A small sacrifice, done without full enthusiasm.

If you want to truly feel what "reluctantly" means — think of a moment in your own life when you had to do something you didn't want to do, but you did it anyway. Maybe you said sorry first in a fight, even though you felt the other person was more at fault. Maybe you went to a dentist you'd been putting off. Maybe you followed a rule you thought was unfair.

That feeling — of doing something while your heart pulls back — is reluctance. And when you describe the action, you say it was done reluctantly.

Reluctantly = doing something despite not wanting to.

The action happens. The willingness does not. Something in between — duty, need, pressure, reason — bridges the gap. That tension, that inner resistance visible in the way something is done, is what "reluctantly" captures perfectly.
13574:
To remand means to send someone or something back — but always in a formal, official, or legal context. It is not a word you use casually in everyday life. It almost exclusively appears in legal and judicial settings.

There are two distinct situations where this word is used. Understanding both will give you the full picture.
Situation 1: Remanding a Person (the most common use)

When a court remands a person, it means the court is ordering that person to be held in custody (kept in jail or a detention facility) while they wait for their trial or for the next stage of their legal proceedings to happen.

Think of it this way: a person has been accused of a crime. They appear before a judge, but the trial isn't happening today — it will happen weeks or months later. The judge must decide: should this person be allowed to go home and wait freely, or should they be locked up until the trial? If the judge decides they should be locked up, the judge remands them. The person is remanded into custody (sometimes simply called being on remand).

Example: "The judge remanded the accused in custody until the trial begins next month."
This means: the judge ordered the accused to be kept in jail until the trial.

Another example: "He was remanded for two weeks before his bail hearing."
This means: he was sent to detention and kept there for two weeks, until the separate hearing about bail.

Important nuance — remanded on bail:
Remanding doesn't always mean going to jail. A court can also remand someone on bail. This means the person is released — allowed to go home — but only under strict conditions (like surrendering their passport, reporting to a police station regularly, or paying a sum of money as a guarantee). They are still technically "remanded" because the court is controlling what happens to them between now and their next appearance. The key idea is the same: the court is managing what happens to this person while the legal process continues.

So to put it simply:

  • Remanded in custody = kept in jail while waiting.
  • Remanded on bail = released but under conditions while waiting.

Both mean the case is not over. The person is in a sort of legal "in-between" state, and the court has decided how they will spend that time.
Situation 2: Remanding a Case (used in higher courts)

The second use involves sending a legal case back to a lower court. This happens in appellate proceedings — when a higher court (like a court of appeal or a supreme court) reviews a decision that was made by a lower court.

If the higher court finds that the lower court made an error — perhaps it applied the wrong law, or failed to consider certain evidence properly — the higher court does not simply fix the problem itself. Instead, it remands the case back to the lower court, with instructions on how to handle it correctly.

Example: "The Supreme Court remanded the case to the lower court for reconsideration."
This means: the Supreme Court sent the case back down to the original court and told it to reconsider the matter, this time following the proper legal principles.

Another example: "The appeals court found errors in the original verdict and remanded the case for a new trial."
This means: the appeals court decided the first trial was flawed, so it sent the case back to be tried again from scratch.
The Thread That Connects Both Uses

You might wonder: how are these two uses related? They both involve sending something back under official authority — in one case, sending a person back into custody or back into a controlled state; in the other, sending a case back to where it originated. The word carries a sense of authority directing something backward through a process, rather than forward to a conclusion.

You'll most often see remand used in the passive voice (where something is done to the person or case):

  • "She was remanded in custody." (The court put her in jail to wait.)
  • "The accused was remanded to appear again on 15 November." (He was ordered to come back to court on that date.)
  • "The matter was remanded to the district court." (The case was sent back down.)

You'll also see the noun form remand used frequently:

  • "He is currently on remand." (He is currently in custody awaiting trial — his case hasn't been decided yet.)
  • "The remand period lasted three weeks." (The time he spent in custody while waiting lasted three weeks.)

It's worth being clear about what remand does not mean:

  • It does not mean the person has been found guilty. A person on remand is still, legally, presumed innocent. They are simply being held or controlled while the legal process plays out.
  • It does not mean the case is over. Remand always implies that there is more to come — a future trial, a future hearing, or further proceedings in a lower court.
  • It is not the same as a sentence. When a judge sentences someone (after they've been convicted), that's a punishment. When a judge remands someone, they are simply deciding what happens to that person in the waiting period before a verdict.

To remand a personTo officially order them into custody (or controlled release on bail) while they await trial or further court proceedings.
To remand a caseFor a higher court to send a case back to a lower court with instructions to reconsider or retry it.

Actually, let me put that in plain words instead:

To remand means: to officially send something or someone back — a person back into custody or controlled release while awaiting legal proceedings, or a case back to a lower court for further handling. The common thread is always official authority sending something backward in a process, not forward to a conclusion.
13575:
A remark is a comment or statement that someone makes — usually briefly — to share a thought, observation, or reaction about something. It's what comes out when a person notices something and says something about it.

It can be spoken or written, and it typically feels spontaneous, conversational, or passing in nature, rather than a long, structured argument or explanation.

She made a remark about the weather.
His remark surprised everyone in the room.
What makes a remark feel like a "remark"

The key character of a remark is that it is short and pointed — it's not a speech, not a full explanation, not a detailed opinion piece. It's a brief verbal or written stab at expressing something: a thought, a feeling, a judgment, a reaction.

Think of it like this: if someone is walking past a painting and says "That's a strange choice of colour" — that's a remark. They didn't stop to give a lecture. They just said something in passing.
Remarks can carry many different tones

A remark by itself is neutral — it just means a comment was made. But remarks are often described with adjectives that tell you the tone:

  • A casual remark — said lightly, without much intention
  • An offhand remark — said without much thought, almost accidentally
  • A passing remark — mentioned briefly, not dwelt upon
  • A sharp / cutting remark — said in a way that stings or criticizes
  • A snide remark — said with a hint of mockery or sarcasm
  • A witty remark — a clever, funny comment
  • A kind remark — something warm and appreciative said to someone
  • A personal remark — a comment directed at someone about them personally (often unwelcome)
  • A pointed remark — a comment that makes a specific, deliberate point, often critically

She made a cutting remark about his work, and he felt deflated.
He threw in a witty remark that made the whole room laugh.

When used in formal contexts, "remarks" (plural) often refers to a brief prepared speech or a set of opening or closing statements delivered by someone at an event, conference, ceremony, or meeting.

The minister delivered his opening remarks at the summit.
She thanked the audience in her closing remarks.

This usage feels slightly elevated and official. Here, "remarks" is essentially a polished, public version of the word — it still means "what someone said," but said with structure and intention in a formal setting.

These are the natural ways "remark" appears in English:

  • make a remark — the standard way to say someone said something
    He made a remark about her new hairstyle.*
  • pass a remark — slightly informal; means to say something, often casually or critically
    She passed a remark that made him uncomfortable.*
  • a remark about / on something — to show what the comment was about
    a remark about politics / a remark on her performance*
  • worthy of remark — formal expression meaning "notable enough to mention"
    The result was barely worthy of remark.*
  • a remark in passing — something said briefly, not as a main point
    He mentioned it as a remark in passing.*

Comment and remark are very close in meaning and are often interchangeable. However:

  • Comment tends to feel slightly more deliberate and can be written (a comment on a document, a social media comment).
  • Remark often feels more spontaneous, verbal, and conversational.

Observation is more about noticing something factually and reporting it neutrally. A remark carries more personality and can carry an attitude or judgment. All observations can become remarks, but not all remarks are objective observations.

Statement is more formal and definitive — it carries weight and intention. A remark is lighter and more fleeting.

Note is often written and supplementary — an addition to something already said or written. A remark is more of a standalone thing said in conversation.

A remark is a brief, expressed thought — a small verbal or written act of saying something about something. It lives in the moment of conversation or speech. It can be kind, cruel, funny, careless, profound, or pointless. What unites all remarks is their quality of being said (or written), briefly, about something that caught the speaker's attention.

When you hear someone say "That's an interesting remark," they mean: someone said something brief but worth thinking about. When you hear "What a rude remark," someone said something brief but hurtful. The word itself doesn't judge — it just tells you a comment was made.
13576:
To remark means to say something as a comment or observation — usually something brief that you've noticed and want to express out loud (or in writing).

The key idea inside the word is this: you noticed something, and now you're giving voice to that observation. It's the moment when a thought you've had becomes a spoken (or written) comment.

She remarked that the room felt unusually quiet.

This tells us she noticed the quietness, and she said so. It wasn't a long speech. It wasn't a formal argument. It was simply a comment she made — a thought she put into words.

In older, more formal, or literary writing, "remark" can also mean simply to notice or observe something — without necessarily saying anything.

He remarked a slight trembling in her hands.

Here, it means: he noticed a slight trembling. No speech is involved. This usage is rare in everyday modern English, but you might encounter it in classic novels or formal writing, so it's good to know.

In daily life, when people use "remark," they almost always mean the first sense — saying something as a comment.
How to Use It — The Sentence Patterns

Pattern 1: remark + that + (what was said)
This is the most common structure.

He remarked that the food was excellent.
She remarked that the train was running late.
The teacher remarked that the students had improved a lot.

Pattern 2: remark + on/upon + (what was noticed)
Here you use "on" or "upon" to point at the thing being commented about.

Everyone remarked on her beautiful dress.
They remarked on how calm the sea looked.
The doctor remarked upon the patient's quick recovery.

Pattern 3: remark used while quoting speech directly
When a speaker's exact words are given, "remarked" appears after them, like a tag.

"This is quite surprising," she remarked.
"The colour doesn't suit the wall," he remarked.
The Feel and Tone of the Word

"Remark" carries a sense of casualness and brevity. When someone remarks something, they are not giving a lecture, not making a formal declaration, and not writing an essay. They're simply giving voice to something they noticed — often in a natural, almost offhand way.

There is also often a mild personal quality to it. A remark usually comes from you — from your own observation of something in the moment. It's your small commentary on the world around you.

Compare:

  • He said the painting was beautiful. → Neutral. Just tells us he spoke these words.
  • He remarked that the painting was beautiful. → Tells us he noticed it, was struck by it, and said so as a comment. There's a small but real difference in feel.

This is where the word truly comes alive — by seeing how it sits among its neighbours.

Say — the most plain, neutral word for speaking. It carries no extra meaning. She said it was cold. No implication of noticing, no particular tone.

Comment — very close to "remark." The two are often interchangeable. But "comment" leans slightly more toward responding to something specific or giving an opinion. She commented on the report suggests she is responding to that report directly. She remarked on the report is a touch more spontaneous, more like a passing observation.

Observe — when used in the sense of speaking, "observe" feels a little more formal and analytical than "remark." He observed that crime had increased sounds like a measured, careful statement. He remarked that crime had increased sounds more like something he said in conversation.

Note — often used in formal or written contexts. She noted that the figures were wrong implies careful, deliberate attention. It's more precise and official-sounding than "remark."

Mention — to mention something is to bring it up briefly, often almost in passing, and not necessarily as a comment on something you've noticed. He mentioned he'd been to London is just saying he brought it up. There's less of a "noticing" quality than in "remark."

Point out — to point out is to specifically draw another person's attention to something, often something they might have missed or overlooked. She pointed out that the back door was unlocked. "Remark" doesn't necessarily target the other person's attention that way — it's simply a comment.

To remark is to look at the world — a situation, a person, an event, an idea — notice something about it, and say something brief about what you've noticed. It's the natural human act of turning a quiet observation into a spoken word.

It is not dramatic. It is not lengthy. It is personal and present — something said in the moment, arising from something seen or felt.

She remarked that the stars were especially bright that night.

That single sentence shows you someone who looked up, noticed something, and quietly said so. That is the verb "remark" at its heart.
13577:
Something remarkable is so unusual, impressive, or exceptional that it naturally makes people stop, notice it, and want to talk about it. It goes well beyond what is normal or expected.

Think of it this way: out of a hundred ordinary things you come across in a day, if one of them is so striking that you feel the urge to point it out to someone and say "did you see that?" — that thing is remarkable.

The word carries a sense of genuine surprise mixed with admiration. When you call something remarkable, you are essentially saying:

"This is not what I usually see. This stands out. This deserves attention."

It is not just "good" or "nice." It is impressively beyond the ordinary — something that leaves a mark in your mind.

"Remarkable" is a strong word, but not the strongest. Here is a rough sense of the scale:

Good → Impressive → Remarkable → Extraordinary → Unbelievable

It sits comfortably above average praise. When you use it, people understand you are genuinely struck by something — not just being polite.

Almost anything that exceeds normal expectations can be called remarkable:

  • A person: She is a remarkable doctor — she has saved thousands of lives.
  • An achievement: Finishing the race after breaking his leg was a remarkable feat.
  • A quality or trait: Her patience with difficult students is truly remarkable.
  • A recovery or change: The city's recovery after the earthquake was remarkable.
  • An object or work: This is a remarkable piece of writing.
  • An event or moment: Meeting them there, by pure chance, was remarkable.

Notice that it can describe people, things, events, qualities, and actions — it is very flexible.

1. Positive (Most Common)

This is when "remarkable" expresses admiration and praise.

"He showed remarkable courage during the crisis."

Here, you are celebrating someone's courage as exceptional and worthy of recognition.

2. Neutral / Purely Noteworthy

Sometimes "remarkable" simply means surprisingly worth noticing, without strong praise or criticism.

"It is remarkable how quickly habits form in children."

Here, the speaker is not praising or criticising — they are just pointing out something striking and worth thinking about.

3. Ironic or Sarcastic (Rare)

Occasionally, people use "remarkable" to express surprise at something surprisingly bad or careless, often with a tone of disbelief.

"It is remarkable how little he prepared for such an important meeting."

The word here highlights the negative through contrast — you would not normally expect such carelessness in that situation. Context and tone make this meaning clear.

In everyday use, you will mostly encounter the positive sense.
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are related but not identical:

  • Notable — worth noticing, but said in a calm, factual way. Less emotionally striking than "remarkable." ("He made some notable contributions to the field.")
  • Impressive — creates a strong reaction in the observer; focuses on your personal feeling of being impressed. ("Her performance was impressive.")
  • Exceptional — means it is an exception to the usual standard; implies very high quality. ("The food was exceptional.")
  • Extraordinary — literally "beyond ordinary"; stronger and more emphatic than remarkable. ("She has an extraordinary gift for music.")
  • Outstanding — stands out above others; often used for performance or achievement. ("He is an outstanding student.")

"Remarkable" feels a little more personal and human than these others. It carries the sense that a real person looked at something, was genuinely struck by it, and felt the need to say something about it. It blends surprise, admiration, and the impulse to point something out to the world.

It almost always appears in one of these patterns:

Pattern 1: It is a [remarkable] + noun

"It is a remarkable achievement."
"She gave a remarkable performance."

Pattern 2: Subject + is/was + remarkable

"His recovery was remarkable."
"The view from the top is truly remarkable."

Pattern 3: Remarkable + how/that + clause

"It is remarkable how calm she stayed under pressure."
"It is remarkable that no one was hurt."

You will often see it strengthened with words like truly, absolutely, quite, or nothing short of:

"Her dedication is truly remarkable."
"The result was nothing short of remarkable."

Remarkable means something is so unusual, impressive, or exceptional that it naturally stands out from everything around it and makes people want to notice and talk about it.

If you remember that single idea — "worth noticing and talking about, in a way that goes beyond the ordinary" — you will always use and understand this word correctly.
13578:
Something is remediable when it can be fixed, corrected, or put right. That's the heart of it.

The word "remediable" comes from the noun remedy — which means a solution, a cure, or a fix. The suffix -able means capable of being. So remediable = capable of being remedied.

Whenever you see the word remediable, the single most important thing it tells you is this: a solution exists, or is at least possible. The problem isn't permanent. It isn't hopeless. Something can be done about it.

The word is applied to a wide range of things — situations, problems, errors, deficiencies, harm, damage, conditions. Essentially, anything that has gone wrong or is lacking in some way could be described as remediable if it can be corrected.

Here are some natural examples across different areas:

  • In education: "The student's gaps in understanding are remediable with extra coaching." → The gaps can be filled; they aren't permanent.
  • In medicine: "The doctor confirmed the condition was remediable with the right treatment." → It can be treated or cured.
  • In law: "The court found the procedural error remediable and allowed the case to continue." → The mistake could be corrected without throwing out the whole case.
  • In the environment: "The pollution in the river, while serious, was described as remediable." → The damage can be undone or reduced.
  • In everyday life: "Fortunately, the damage caused by the misunderstanding was remediable." → Things could be repaired between the people involved.
The Most Important Nuance: It Signals Hope

The real weight of "remediable" is emotional and practical — it carries the idea that the situation is not lost. When something is described as remediable, there's a sense of relief, optimism, or at least reassurance. The speaker is saying: This is bad, yes — but it's not beyond saving.

This is what gives the word its power. It's not just a dry technical fact. It's a signal about the future — that recovery, correction, or improvement is within reach.

It does not mean:

  • The problem is easy to fix (it could be very hard — just still possible)
  • The problem has already been fixed (it only means it can be)
  • The problem is minor or unimportant (a very serious problem can still be remediable)

So remediable answers only one question: Is a fix possible? The answer is yes. How hard, how expensive, how long it takes — none of that is part of the word's meaning.

The most important contrast you'll encounter is the word irremediable — which means exactly the opposite: cannot be fixed, corrected, or undone. Permanent. Beyond repair.

RemediableA fix is possible
IrremediableNo fix is possible — it's permanent

For example:

  • "The hearing loss was irremediable." → It cannot be restored; it's permanent.
  • "The hearing loss was remediable with the proper hearing aids and therapy." → Something can be done.

Understanding this pair together gives you full command of both words.

Remediable is a formal word. You're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Legal documents and judgments
  • Medical reports
  • Academic writing
  • Professional evaluations
  • Policy and governance discussions

In casual conversation, people would more naturally say fixable, correctable, or curable depending on context. But remediable is the formal, precise, all-purpose version that works across all these domains.
Close Synonyms — and How They Differ

Several words are close to remediable, but each has a slightly different flavour:

  • Fixable — casual, general-purpose. "The car is fixable."
  • Correctable — often used for errors, mistakes, inaccuracies.
  • Curable — almost exclusively for medical conditions.
  • Rectifiable — formal, often used for wrongs, errors, or injustices.
  • Repairable — usually for physical or tangible damage.

Remediable is the broadest and most formal of these. It can be used for all of the above contexts — mistakes, harm, medical conditions, physical damage, social wrongs — without sounding out of place.
A Quick Way to Remember It

Remedy → Remediable = "a remedy is possible."

Whenever you see the word, ask yourself: Can this be remedied? If yes, it's remediable. That's the whole meaning — elegant, precise, and hopeful.
13579: Remedial means designed to fix, correct, or improve a problem, weakness, or deficiency. Think of the word "remedy" — a cure or solution to a problem. "Remedial" is simply its adjective form, describing anything that acts as that cure or corrective solution. If something is remedial, its entire purpose is to address what is lacking, broken, or below standard.

1. In Education (the most common use)

This is where most people first encounter this word. A remedial class, remedial course, or remedial program is one specifically designed for students who have fallen behind the expected level in a subject. These students haven't yet mastered what others at their level have, so the remedial class focuses on rebuilding that missing foundation before moving forward.

For example, a university might offer a remedial writing course for students whose grammar and composition skills aren't yet at college level. A school might run a remedial reading program for children who are struggling with literacy while their peers are progressing normally.

A crucial point here: being in a remedial class says nothing about a person's intelligence. It simply means they have a specific gap in knowledge or skill that needs targeted attention. The class exists to close that gap, not to label the student.

2. In General Use — medical, professional, legal, everyday contexts

Outside of education, "remedial" is used broadly to describe any action, treatment, measure, or work that is taken in order to correct a fault or problem. Here, the word is entirely neutral and technical — there's no judgment attached whatsoever.

Some examples across different fields:

  • Remedial action — steps taken to fix or correct a problem. ("The factory was ordered to take immediate remedial action after the safety inspection revealed serious hazards.")
  • Remedial treatment — medical or therapeutic treatment aimed at fixing or healing something. ("After his knee surgery, he was prescribed a series of remedial exercises to restore strength and mobility.")
  • Remedial work — repair or corrective work done on something damaged or faulty. ("Following the flood, remedial work was carried out on the structural damage to the building.")
  • Remedial measures — steps or policies put in place to correct a bigger problem. ("The government introduced remedial measures to address the rise in air pollution.")

In all of these cases, the common thread is the same: something is wrong or lacking, and the remedial thing is the deliberate effort to fix it.
The Connotation — How the Word "Feels" in Different Situations

This is where the word gets a little nuanced, and understanding this will help you use it correctly and read it accurately.

Neutral to formal contexts: In professional, medical, legal, and corporate language, "remedial" carries zero emotional weight. It is a clean, clinical term that simply means "corrective." A legal document referring to "remedial measures" is simply describing steps taken to fix a violation. No shame, no stigma — just precision.

Sensitive in education: When applied to students or classes, the word can feel slightly uncomfortable or even stigmatizing, because being identified as needing "remedial" help can imply that a person is below average or not keeping up. This is why many schools and universities today prefer softer alternatives like foundational courses, developmental classes, or support programs — they mean the same thing but carry less of a stigma. So while "remedial" in education is not wrong to use, be aware that it can feel loaded, and in sensitive conversations it's worth considering whether a gentler phrase is more appropriate.

Informal/mocking use: In casual speech, someone might say something like "That's so remedial" or "Don't be remedial" to mockingly suggest that a person or idea is embarrassingly basic, slow, or beneath a certain standard. This usage is informal and dismissive in tone. It's not something you'd see in a textbook or formal document — it's slang, and it's often unkind.
The One Test to Always Get It Right

Whenever you encounter the word "remedial," ask yourself this simple question: Is this thing trying to fix, correct, or address a weakness or deficiency? If the answer is yes, then "remedial" is exactly the right word. The deficiency might be a student's knowledge gap, a weakened muscle after injury, a cracked building after an earthquake, or a company's failed policy — but in every single case, what makes something "remedial" is that its purpose is correction.

• "He was enrolled in remedial math to catch up before entering the main course." (correcting a knowledge gap)
  • "The doctor recommended remedial physiotherapy for her shoulder injury." (correcting a physical problem)
  • "The city council approved remedial measures to repair the aging water pipes." (correcting infrastructure failure)
  • "After the scandal, the organization underwent remedial training on workplace ethics." (correcting behavior/culture)

In every case, something is wrong — and the remedial thing is the deliberate, structured effort to make it right.
